details: Working, about 10% of your pay goes to tax. In retirement, the plan shows 0% on withdrawals.
Draw on taxable savings first, then pre-tax accounts like your 401(k), and Roth accounts last. Your savings are about 67% pre-tax, 31% Roth, and 2% taxable and cash.

finding.headline: At age 50, you can contribute more to a 401(k) each year, and Social Security grows if you wait past full retirement age.
details: For 2027, people aged 50 and over who take part in most 401(k) plans can contribute up to $34,000 each year. That includes the $8,500 catch-up amount, which is up from $8,000 for 2026.
Social Security benefits rise for each month you wait past full retirement age, but the increase stops at age 70. Your plan to retire at age 66 falls between these two points.
Plan to sign up for Medicare at age 65, which is 15 years away. If you wait past 65, your Medicare coverage may be delayed and cost more.

finding.headline: You can count on $19,500 a year: $15,000 for basics and $4,500 for the rest.
details: Your basics cost about $15,000 a year.
Your spending goal is $15,000 a year, and it lasted in 100 of 100 market scenarios.

assumptions: All figures are in today's dollars: what money buys now, not the larger sums prices will reach.

Savings grow on average 5.0% a year above inflation in stocks and 1.8% in bonds, with good and bad years. The plan tests many possible market paths. These are planning figures, not a forecast. They are fixed, so every plan is tested on the same markets; to see a bad stretch, try a What If such as markets fall 30%.

Until you retire you save about $1,497 a year: what your take-home pay leaves after your spending now, which is less than the saving you gave, plus $600 from your employer's match. If that is wrong, change 'Yearly saving' or your spending now in your answers.
Pay stays at today's level until you retire, with no raises. This is fixed: raises are not certain, so the plan does not count on them. If your pay changes, change it in your answers.
Social Security uses the figure you gave, read as the benefit at 67. Your answers show $14,400 a year from 67. This plan starts it at 69, which pays about $16,700 a year.
If you retire before Medicare starts at 65, health cover costs about $10,000 a person a year until then (an assumption). Other health costs follow CMS figures by age.

Tax uses the 2027 federal brackets, the standard deduction and your state's rates. While you work, 401(k) saving comes off taxable pay. In retirement the plan counts 85% of Social Security as taxable, the most the law allows, so the tax may be a little high.
The plan runs to age 92. There is about a 1 in 4 chance that you will live that long (US life table, SOA 2024). People with more money tend to live longer than that table says.
